Abstract.

We construct motives over the rational numbers associated with symmetric power moments of Kloosterman sums, and prove that their LL-functions extend meromorphically to the complex plane and satisfy a functional equation conjectured by Broadhurst and Roberts. Although the motives in question turn out to be “classical”, we compute their Hodge numbers by means of the irregular Hodge filtration on their realizations as exponential mixed Hodge structures. We show that all Hodge numbers are either zero or one, which implies potential automorphy thanks to recent results of Patrikis and Taylor.

1. Introduction

This paper is devoted to the study of a family of global LL-functions built up by assembling symmetric power moments of Kloosterman sums over finite fields. We prove that they arise from potentially automorphic motives over the rational numbers, and hence admit a meromorphic extension to the complex plane that satisfies the expected functional equation. The exact shape of the latter was conjectured by Broadhurst and Roberts.

1.1. LL-functions of symmetric power moments of Kloosterman sums

Let pp be a prime number, 𝐅p\mathbf{F}_{p} the finite field with pp elements, and 𝐅¯p\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p} an algebraic closure of 𝐅p\mathbf{F}_{p}. If qq is a power of pp, we denote by 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q} the subfield of 𝐅¯p\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p} with qq elements and by tr𝐅q/𝐅p:𝐅q→𝐅p\tr_{\mathbf{F}_{q}/\mathbf{F}_{p}}\colon\mathbf{F}_{q}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{F}_{p} its trace map. Let ψ:𝐅p→𝐂×\psi\colon\mathbf{F}_{p}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{C}^{\times} be a non-trivial additive character. For each a∈𝐅q×a\in\mathbf{F}_{q}^{\times}, the Kloosterman sum is the real number

(1.1) Kl2⁡(a;q)=∑x∈𝐅q×ψ⁡(tr𝐅q/𝐅p​(x+a/x)).\Kl_{2}(a;q)=\sum_{x\in\mathbf{F}_{q}^{\times}}\psi(\mathrm{tr}_{\mathbf{F}_{q}/\penalty\mathbf{F}_{p}}(x+{a}/{x})).

As an application of the Riemann hypothesis for curves over finite fields [62], Weil proved that there exist algebraic integers αa,βa\alpha_{a},\beta_{a} of absolute value q\sqrt{q} satisfying Kl2⁡(a;q)=−(αa+βa)\Kl_{2}(a;q)=-(\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a}) and αa​βa=q\alpha_{a}\beta_{a}=q. For each integer k⩾1k\geqslant 1, we define kk-th symmetric powers of Kloosterman sums

Kl2Symk⁡(a;q)=∑i=0kαai​βak−i\Kl_{2}^{\Sym^{k}}(a;q)=\sum_{i=0}^{k}\alpha_{a}^{i}\beta_{a}^{k-i}\vskip-3.0pt

and, summing over all aa, we form the moments

m2k​(q)=∑a∈𝐅q×Kl2Symk⁡(a;q).m_{2}^{k}(q)=\sum_{a\in\mathbf{F}_{q}^{\times}}\Kl^{\Sym^{k}}_{2}(a;q).

Note that this convention makes Kl2Sym1⁡(a;q)\Kl_{2}^{\Sym^{1}}(a;q) opposite to Kl2⁡(a,q)\Kl_{2}(a;q). Contrary to Kloosterman sums and their symmetric powers, the moments m2k​(q)m_{2}^{k}(q) are rational integers that do not depend on the choice of the additive character. We pack them into the generating series

Zk​(p,T)=exp⁡(∑n=1∞m2k​(pn)​Tnn),Z_{k}(p;T)=\exp\biggl(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}m_{2}^{k}(p^{n})\frac{T^{n}}{n}\biggr),

which in fact turns out to be a polynomial with integer coefficients. The first few cases are easy to compute: both Z1​(p,T)Z_{1}(p;T) and Z2​(p,T)Z_{2}(p;T) are equal to 1−T1-T, and the equalities

Z3​(p,T)=(1−T)​(1−(p3)​p2​T),Z4​(p,T)={1−T if ​p=2,(1−T)​(1−p2​T) if ​p>2,Z_{3}(p;T)=(1-T)(1-\left(\tfrac{p}{3}\right)p^{2}T),\qquad Z_{4}(p;T)=\begin{cases}1-T&\text{ if }p=2,\\ (1-T)(1-p^{2}T)&\text{ if }p>2,\end{cases}

hold, where (p/3)(p/3) stands for the Legendre symbol. From this one may already infer that the polynomial Zk​(p,T)Z_{k}(p;T) is always divisible by 1−T1-T. Other so-called “trivial factors” appear when kk is a multiple of 44 or when kk is even and pp is small compared with kk, see Section 5.1.1 infra. Better behaved than Zk​(p,T)Z_{k}(p;T) is the polynomial Mk​(p,T)M_{k}(p;T) obtained by removing these trivial factors, since all its roots then have the same absolute value p−(k+1)/2p^{-{(k+1)}/{2}}.

We shall now build a global LL-function over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} with the above polynomials as local Euler factors. We first discuss the case of odd symmetric powers, say of the form k=2​m+1k=2m+1. Let SS be the set of odd prime numbers smaller than or equal to kk. For all p∉Sp\notin S, define the local factor at pp as Lk​(p,s)=Mk​(p,p−s)−1L_{k}(p;s)=M_{k}(p;p^{-s})^{-1} and consider the Euler product

Lk​(s)=∏p∉SLk​(p,s),L_{k}(s)=\prod_{p\notin S}L_{k}(p;s),

which by the previous remark about the roots of Mk​(p,T)M_{k}(p;T) converges absolutely on the half-plane Re⁡(s)>(k+3)/2\mathrm{Re}(s)>{(k+3)}/{2}. This function is expected to have meromorphic continuation to the entire complex plane and satisfy a functional equation relating its values at ss and k+2−sk+2-s. As usual, the functional equation has a neat formulation after completing the LL-function by adding local factors at p∈Sp\in S, as we shall do in (5.14) infra, and gamma factors at infinity. We set 𝔑k=1s3s5s⋯ks\mathfrak{N}_{k}=1_{\mathrm{s}}3_{\mathrm{s}}5_{\mathrm{s}}\cdots k_{\mathrm{s}}, where nsn_{\mathrm{s}} denotes the square-free part of an integer nn (i.e., the product of all prime numbers pp such that the pp-adic valuation vp​(n)v_{p}(n) is odd), and we consider the complete LL-function

Λk​(s)=(𝔑kπm)s/2​∏j=1mΓ⁡(s−j2)​∏p​ primeLk​(p,s).\Lambda_{k}(s)=\Bigl(\frac{\mathfrak{N}_{k}}{\pi^{m}}\Bigr)^{{s}/{2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Gamma\Bigl(\frac{s-j}{2}\Bigr)\prod_{p\text{\ prime}}L_{k}(p;s).
Theorem 1.2.

Assume kk is odd. The function Lk​(s)L_{k}(s) admits a meromorphic continuation to the complex plane and satisfies the functional equation

Λk​(s)=Λk​(k+2−s).\Lambda_{k}(s)=\Lambda_{k}(k+2-s).

A similar result holds for even symmetric powers, except that we were unable to make the local invariants explicit at p=2p=2. To formulate the statement, we write either k=2​m+4k=2m+4 or k=2​m+2k=2m+2 with mm an even integer, and we define SS as the set of all prime numbers smaller than or equal to k/2k/2. The local factors at odd primes in SS are described in (5.24) infra. Besides, we set 𝔑′k=2u4u6u⋯ku\mathfrak{N}^{\prime}_{k}=2_{\mathrm{u}}4_{\mathrm{u}}6_{\mathrm{u}}\cdots k_{\mathrm{u}}, where nun_{\mathrm{u}} denotes the odd part of the radical of an integer nn (i.e., the product of all odd primes dividing nn). We then complete the LL-function outside the prime 22 as follows:

Λk′​(s)=(𝔑k′πm)s/2​∏j=1mΓ⁡(s−j2)​∏p≠2Lk​(p,s).\Lambda^{\prime}_{k}(s)=\Bigl(\frac{\mathfrak{N}_{k}^{\prime}}{\pi^{m}}\Bigr)^{{s}/{2}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}\Gamma\Bigl(\frac{s-j}{2}\Bigr)\prod_{p\neq 2}L_{k}(p;s).
Theorem 1.3.

Assume kk is even. The function Lk​(s)L_{k}(s) meromorphically extends to the complex plane. Moreover, there exists a sign εk∈{±1}\varepsilon_{k}\in\{\pm 1\}, an integer rk⩾0r_{k}\geqslant 0, and a reciprocal of a polynomial with rational coefficients Lk​(2,T)L_{k}(2;T) such that, setting Λk​(s)=2rk​s/2​Lk​(2,2−s)​Λk′​(s)\Lambda_{k}(s)=2^{{r_{k}s}/{2}}L_{k}(2;2^{-s})\Lambda_{k}^{\prime}(s), the following functional equation holds:

Λk​(s)=εk​Λk​(k+2−s).\Lambda_{k}(s)=\varepsilon_{k}\Lambda_{k}(k+2-s).

The above formulas for Λk​(s)\Lambda_{k}(s) match the numerical observations made by Broadhurst and Roberts in [5, Eq. (128)] and [6, 47], up to replacing their variable ss with s−2s-2 due to a Tate twist. For even kk, they also conjecture that the elusive invariants take the values rk=⌊k/6⌋r_{k}=\left\lfloor{k}/{6}\right\rfloor and εk=(−1)tk\varepsilon_{k}=(-1)^{t_{k}}, with tkt_{k} given by the formula

tk=⌊k/8⌋+∑p≡1​(mod​ 4)⌊k/2​p⌋+∑p≡3​(mod​ 4)⌊k/4​p⌋+δ8​𝐙​(k),t_{k}=\left\lfloor{k}/{8}\right\rfloor+\sum_{p\equiv 1\,(\mathrm{mod}\,4)}\left\lfloor{k}/{2p}\right\rfloor+\sum_{p\equiv 3\,(\mathrm{mod}\,4)}\left\lfloor{k}/{4p}\right\rfloor+\delta_{8\mathbf{Z}}(k),

where δ8​𝐙\delta_{8\mathbf{Z}} is the characteristic function of multiples of 88. We explain in 5.3.1 infra how the last three terms above fit with the local computations at odd primes in SS and at infinity.

Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 were previously only known for k⩽8k\leqslant 8. The first four cases are straightforward, as the LL-function is trivial for k=1,2,4k=1,2,4 and agrees, for k=3k=3, with the shifted Dirichlet LL-function L⁡(χ3,s−2)L(\chi_{3},s-2) of the non-trivial quadratic character modulo 33. In the next four cases, the LL-function can be expressed in terms of a Hecke cusp form for some congruence subgroup Γ0​(N)\Gamma_{0}(N) of SL2​(𝐙)\mathrm{SL}_{2}(\mathbf{Z}), as indicated in Table 1 below.

1.2. Cohomological interpretation

After Deligne [9], Kloosterman sums arise as traces of Frobenius acting on an étale local system on the torus 𝔾m,𝐅p\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\mathbf{F}_{p}}. Let ℓ\ell be a prime number distinct from pp and let 𝐐¯ℓ\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell} be an algebraic closure of the field of ℓ\ell-adic numbers. Once we view the character ψ\psi as taking values in 𝐐¯ℓ\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell} by choosing a primitive pp-th root of unity in this field, there is a rank one ℓ\ell-adic local system ℒψ\mathscr{L}_{\psi} on the affine line 𝔸𝐅p1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\mathbf{F}_{p}} with trace function z↦ψ⁡(tr𝐅q/𝐅p⁡(z))z\mapsto\psi(\tr_{\mathbf{F}_{q}/\mathbf{F}_{p}}(z)), the so-called Artin-Schreier sheaf. where, if xx and zz are coordinates on 𝔾m,𝐅p2\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\mathbf{F}_{p}}^{2}, the function ff is given by x+z/xx+z/x and π\pi stands for the projection to the zz-coordinate. That is, we set

Kl2=Rπ!f∗ℒψ[1].\Kl_{2}=\mathrm{R}\pi_{!}f^{\ast}\mathscr{L}_{\psi}[1].

Deligne showed that the object Kl2\Kl_{2} is concentrated in degree zero, and that it is a rank-two lisse sheaf on 𝔾m,𝐅p\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\mathbf{F}_{p}} tamely ramified at zero, wildly ramified at infinity, and pure of weight one. Indeed, the “forget supports” map Rπ!f∗ℒψ→Rπ∗f∗ℒψ\mathrm{R}\pi_{!}f^{\ast}\mathscr{L}_{\psi}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathrm{R}\pi_{\ast}f^{\ast}\mathscr{L}_{\psi} is an isomorphism. Grothendieck’s trace formula and base change yield the equalities

Kl2⁡(a,q)=−tr⁡(Froba|Kl2)=−(αa+βa),\Kl_{2}(a,q)=-\tr(\mathrm{Frob}_{a}|\Kl_{2})=-(\alpha_{a}+\beta_{a}),

where αa\alpha_{a} and βa\beta_{a} are the eigenvalues of Frobenius acting on a geometric fiber of Kl2\Kl_{2} above aa. In the same vein, symmetric powers of Kloosterman sums are local traces of Frobenius on the symmetric powers Symk⁡Kl2\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}. To obtain the moments, we consider the action of geometric Frobenius FpF_{p} on the étale cohomology with compact support of Symk⁡Kl2\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}. Since it is concentrated in degree one, invoking the trace formula again we get the equality

(1.5) Zk​(p,T)=det(1−Fp​T∣Hét,c1​(𝔾m,𝐅¯p,Symk⁡Kl2)).Z_{k}(p;T)=\det\Bigl(1-F_{p}T\mid\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\textup{\'{e}t},{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})\Bigr).

It follows that Zk​(p,T)Z_{k}(p;T) is a polynomial with integer coefficients of degree minus the Euler characteristic of the sheaf Symk⁡Kl2\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2} which, by the Grothendieck-Ogg-Shafarevich formula, is equal to its Swan conductor at infinity. Fu and Wan computed it for odd primes pp in [21], completing partial results by Robba [46]:

deg⁡Zk​(p,T)=Sw∞​(Symk⁡Kl2)={k+12−⌊k2​p+12⌋ if ​k​ odd,k2−⌊k2​p⌋ if ​k​ even.\deg Z_{k}(p;T)=\mathrm{Sw}_{\infty}(\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k+1}{2}-\left\lfloor\dfrac{k}{2p}+\dfrac{1}{2}\right\rfloor&\text{ if }k\text{ odd,}\\[10.0pt] \dfrac{k}{2}-\left\lfloor\dfrac{k}{2p}\right\rfloor&\text{ if }k\text{ even.}\end{cases}

The remaining case p=2p=2 was treated by Yun, who proved that the Swan conductor is equal to (k+1)/2{(k+1)}/{2} if kk is odd and to ⌊(k+2)/4⌋\left\lfloor{(k+2)}/{4}\right\rfloor if kk is even [64]. Observe that, when pp is large compared with kk, the degree takes the uniform value ⌊(k+1)/2⌋\left\lfloor{(k+1)}/{2}\right\rfloor. The sets SS from Section 1.1 consist exactly of those prime numbers pp at which the degree drops.

From this perspective, the trivial factors of the polynomial Zk​(p,T)Z_{k}(p;T) are accounted for the invariants and the coinvariants of the inertia action at zero and infinity. By “removing them”, we mean replacing étale cohomology with compact support in the right-hand side of (1.5) with middle extension cohomology, which is defined as

Hét,mid1(𝔾m,𝐅¯p,SymkKl2)=im[Hét,c1(𝔾m,𝐅¯p,SymkKln+1)⟶Hét1(𝔾m,𝐅¯p,SymkKln+1)].\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\textup{\'{e}t},{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})=\image\bigl[\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\textup{\'{e}t},{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\textup{\'{e}t}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1})\bigr].

The terminology is coherent with the fact that, letting j:𝔾m↪ℙ1j\colon\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{P}^{1} denote the inclusion, the above image agrees with the cohomology on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} of the intermediate (aka middle) extension sheaf j!∗SymkKl2j_{!\ast}\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}. By definition, Mk​(p,T)M_{k}(p;T) is the polynomial

Mk​(p,T)=det(1−Fp​T∣Hét,mid1​(𝔾m,𝐅¯p,Symk⁡Kl2)).M_{k}(p;T)=\det\Bigl(1-F_{p}T\mid\mathrm{H}^{1}_{\textup{\'{e}t},{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\overline{\mathbf{F}}_{p}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})\Bigr).

Since the étale cohomology and the étale cohomology with compact support of Symk⁡Kl2\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2} have weights ⩾k+1\geqslant k+1 and ⩽k+1\leqslant k+1 respectively by the main theorem of Weil II [11], the middle extension cohomology is pure of weight k+1k+1. What was called mm in Section 1.1 supra is the degree of Mk​(p,T)M_{k}(p;T), that is, the dimension of the middle extension cohomology for all p∉Sp\notin S.

1.3. Exponential Hodge structures and irregular Hodge filtration

Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 are proved by constructing a compatible system of potentially automorphic Galois representations

(1.6) rk,ℓ:Gal⁡(𝐐¯/𝐐)⟶GLm⁡(𝐐ℓ),r_{k,\ell}\colon\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q})\longrightarrow\GL_{m}(\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}),

with ℓ\ell running over all prime numbers, such that rk,ℓr_{k,\ell} is unramified at primes p≠ℓp\neq\ell outside SS and has traces of Frobenius

(1.7) tr⁡(rk,ℓ​(Frobp))={−m2k​(p)−1 if ​4∤k,−m2k​(p)−1−pk/2 if ​4|k(p∉S∪{ℓ}).\mathrm{tr}(r_{k,\ell}(\mathrm{Frob}_{p}))=\begin{cases}-m_{2}^{k}(p)-1&\text{ if }4\nmid k,\\ -m_{2}^{k}(p)-1-p^{{k}/{2}}&\text{ if }4\mid k\end{cases}\qquad(p\notin S\cup\{\ell\}).

The search for such Galois representations was initiated by Fu and Wan, who showed in [22] that LL-functions of symmetric power moments of Kloosterman sums can be realized as Hasse-Weil zeta functions of virtual schemes over Spec⁡𝐙\Spec\mathbf{Z}. An actual Galois representation with traces (1.7) was first constructed by Yun [64] as a subquotient of the étale cohomology of a smooth projective variety over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} cut off the affine Grassmannian of GL2\GL_{2}.

Our construction is instead inspired by the theory of exponential motives, as developed by the first author and Jossen [19]. In a nutshell, this is a theory of motives for pairs (X,f)(X,f) consisting of a smooth variety XX over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and a regular function ff on XX that enriches the de Rham cohomology of the vector bundle with connection Ef=(𝒪X,d+d​f)E^{f}=(\mathscr{O}_{X},{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}f), that is,

HdRn(X,Ef)=𝐇n(X,𝒪X→d+d​fΩX1→d+d​fΩX2⟶⋯).\mathrm{H}^{n}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(X,E^{f})=\mathbf{H}^{n}\Bigl(X,\mathscr{O}_{X}\mathchoice{\xrightarrow{\textstyle\kern 4.0pt{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}f\kern 3.0pt}}{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}f}}{{\longrightarrow}}}{}{}\Omega^{1}_{X}\mathchoice{\xrightarrow{\textstyle\kern 4.0pt{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}f\kern 3.0pt}}{\stackrel{{\scriptstyle{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}f}}{{\longrightarrow}}}{}{}\Omega^{2}_{X}\longrightarrow\cdots\Bigr).

We shall also consider the de Rham cohomology with compact support HdR,cn​(X,Ef)\mathrm{H}^{n}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}(X,E^{f}) and the middle de Rham cohomology HdR,midn​(X,Ef)\mathrm{H}^{n}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}(X,E^{f}), defined as the image of the latter in the former under the “forget supports” map. When ff is the zero function, HdRn​(X,Ef)\mathrm{H}^{n}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(X,E^{f}) is the usual de Rham cohomology of XX and one can indeed prove that Nori motives, one of the candidates for the abelian category of mixed motives, form a full subcategory of exponential motives. However, the function does not need to be identically zero for an a priori exponential motive to be classical. For instance, this is always the case for an exponential motive of the form Hn​(X×𝔸1,t​f)\mathrm{H}^{n}(X\times\mathbb{A}^{\!1},tf). If the zero locus Z={f=0}Z=\{f=0\} is smooth, it is isomorphic to Hn−2​(Z)​(−1)\mathrm{H}^{n-2}(Z)(-1), which should be thought of as a cohomological shadow of the identity

∫0∞∫T⁡(γ)e−t​f​ω​𝑑t=2​π​𝗂​∫γResZ​(ω/f),\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{T(\gamma)}e^{-tf}\omega\,{\mathrm{d}}t=2\pi\mathsf{i}\int_{\gamma}\mathrm{Res}_{Z}({\omega}/{f}),

where ω\omega is a differential form on the complement of ZZ and T⁡(γ)T(\gamma) is the tube of a chain γ\gamma in ZZ. In general, the existence of square roots of the Tate motive 𝐐⁡(−1)\mathbf{Q}(-1) prevents exponential motives from having realizations in mixed Hodge structures, but they do realize into certain mixed Hodge modules over the affine line that Kontsevich and Soibelman call exponential mixed Hodge structures [36]. It will be enough for our purposes to work in this category, whose main properties are summarized in the appendix.

In analogy with the ℓ\ell-adic setting, the Kloosterman connection Kl2\Kl_{2} on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} over a field of characteristic zero is defined by keeping the same diagram (1.4) but replacing the Artin-Schreier sheaf with the differential equation of the exponential. The pullback f∗​ℒψf^{\ast}\mathscr{L}_{\psi} then becomes Ef=(𝒪𝔾m2,d+d​f)E^{f}=(\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{2}},{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}f) and one sets

Kl2=π+​Ef,\Kl_{2}=\pi_{+}E^{f},

which can be thought of as the family of exponential motives H1​(𝔾m,x+z/x)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},x+{z}/{x}) parametrized by z∈𝔾mz\in\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}. Over the complex numbers, Kl2\Kl_{2} is the rank-two vector bundle with connection associated with the modified Bessel differential equation d2​y/d​z2+(1/z)​d​y/d​z−y=0{{\mathrm{d}}^{2}y}/{{\mathrm{d}}z^{2}}+({1}/{z}){{\mathrm{d}}y}/{{\mathrm{d}}z}-y=0, which is indeed the one the exponential periods of H1​(𝔾m,x+z/x)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},x+{z}/{x}) satisfy. Note that this equation has a regular singularity at zero and an irregular singularity at infinity. We can then form the symmetric powers Symk⁡Kl2\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2} and consider the various flavors of de Rham cohomology

HdR1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2),HdR,c1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2),HdR,mid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2),\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}),\qquad\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}),\qquad\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}),

where the last space agrees again with the cohomology of the intermediate extension computed on ℙ1\mathbb{P}^{1} (Corollary 2.15). These vector spaces admit an exponential-Hodge-theoretic interpretation as de Rham fibers of exponential mixed Hodge structures, respectively denoted by

H1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2),Hc1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2),Hmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2).\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}),\qquad\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}),\qquad\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}).

As such, they carry an irregular Hodge filtration, constructed in [50, §6] by extending an idea of Deligne [12]. On the other hand, we shall prove in Theorem 3.2 that these exponential mixed Hodge structures are indeed classical mixed Hodge structures. When this is the case, the irregular Hodge filtration agrees with the usual Hodge filtration, as we show in Proposition A.13, so we can rely on the geometric interpretation of the former to compute the latter.

Theorem 1.8.

The mixed Hodge structure H1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) has weights ⩾k+1\geqslant k+1 and the following numerical data:

  1. (1)

    For odd kk, it is mixed of weights k+1k+1 and 2​k+22k+2, with

    dimH1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)p,q={1if ​p+q=k+1​ and ​p∈{2,4,…,k−1},1if ​p=q=k+1,0otherwise.\dim\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})^{p,q}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }p+q=k+1\text{ and }p\in\{2,4,\dots,k-1\},\\ 1&\text{if }p=q=k+1,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}
  2. (2)

    For even kk, it is mixed of weights k+1k+1 and 2​k+22k+\penalty 2 if k≡2mod4k\equiv 2\bmod 4, and of weights k+1k+1, k+2,k+2, and 2​k+22k+2 if k≡0mod4k\equiv 0\bmod 4, with

    dimH1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)p,q={1if ​p+q=k+1​ and ​min⁡{p,q}∈{2,4,…,2​⌊(k−1)/4⌋},1if p=q=k/2+1 and k≡0mod4,1if ​p=q=k+1,0otherwise.\dim\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})^{p,q}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }p+q=k+1\text{ and }\min\{p,q\}\in\bigl\{2,4,\dots,2\left\lfloor{(k-1)}/{4}\right\rfloor\bigr\},\\ 1&\text{if $p=q={k}/{2}+1$ and $k\equiv 0\bmod 4$},\\ 1&\text{if }p=q=k+1,\\ 0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Furthermore, the mixed Hodge structure Hmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) is pure of weight k+1k+1 and is equal to Wk+1​H1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)W_{k+1}\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}).

To prove that H1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) carries a mixed Hodge structure and compute its Hodge numbers, we first establish the analogous result for the pullback Kl~2\widetilde{\Kl}_{2} of Kl2\Kl_{2} by the double cover of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}. The symmetric power Symk⁡Kl~2\Sym^{k}\widetilde{\Kl}_{2} turns out to be the restriction of the Fourier transform of a 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module on 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} that underlies a pure Hodge module and, as we explain in Section A.7, the theory of mixed Hodge modules endows its cohomology with a mixed Hodge structure whose numerical invariants can be computed in terms of nearby cycles. On the other hand, seeing the cohomology of symmetric powers as the alternating part of the cohomology of tensor powers and using a refined form of the Künneth formula, we get an isomorphism

(1.9) HdR1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)≃HdR1​(𝔾m,Kl2⊗k)sign≃HdRk+1​(𝔾mk+1,Efk)sign,\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})\simeq\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Kl_{2}^{\otimes k})^{\mathrm{sign}}\simeq\mathrm{H}^{k+1}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k+1},E^{f_{k}})^{\mathrm{sign}},

where fkf_{k} is the function x1+⋯+xk+z⁡(1/x1+⋯+1/xk)x_{1}+\cdots+x_{k}+z({1}/{x_{1}}+\cdots+{1}/{x_{k}}) and sign denotes the eigenspace on which the symmetric group 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} acts through the sign. After pullback by the cover t↦z=t2t\mapsto z=t^{2} and the change of coordinates xi=t​yix_{i}=ty_{i}, the function fkf_{k} takes the form f~k=t​g⊞k\widetilde{f}_{k}=tg^{\boxplus k}, where g⊞kg^{\boxplus k} is the kk-fold Thom-Sebastiani sum g⁡(y1)+⋯+g⁡(yk)g(y_{1})+\cdots+g(y_{k}) of the function g⁡(y)=y+1/yg(y)=y+1/y with itself. The cohomology group (1.9) is hence also given by the invariants of

(1.10) HdR1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl~2)≃HdR1​(𝔾mk+1,Et​g⊞k)sign\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\widetilde{\Kl}_{2})\simeq\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{dR}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k+1},E^{tg^{\boxplus k}})^{\mathrm{sign}}

under the action of μ2\mu_{2} coming from the cover. On toric varieties such as a compactification of 𝔾mk\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k} adapted to the function fkf_{k}, the work of Adolphson and Sperber [2] and the results of [15, 63] lead to a geometric interpretation of the irregular Hodge filtration that, once we know the Hodge numbers of (1.10), enables us to complete the proof of Theorem 1.8.

From this circle of ideas we also see that the Hodge structure Hmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) has motivic origin, in the sense that it is cut out of the cohomology of an algebraic variety. Indeed, replacing with 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} the copy of 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} with coordinate tt in 𝔾mk+1\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k+1} and combining the Gysin and the localization long exact sequences, we obtain the following description in Theorem 3.8: let 𝒦⊂𝔾mk\mathscr{K}\subset\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k} be the zero locus of g⊞kg^{\boxplus k}, on which the group 𝔖k×μ2\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{2} acts by permuting the coordinates and sending yiy_{i} to −yi-y_{i}. Then there is an isomorphism of pure Hodge structures

(1.11) Hmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)≅grk−1W​Hck−1​(𝒦)sign×μ2​(−1).\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})\cong\gr_{k-1}^{W}\mathrm{H}^{k-1}_{{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathscr{K})^{\mathrm{sign}\times\mu_{2}}(-1).

For odd kk, the hypersurface 𝒦\mathscr{K} is smooth and we also obtain an isomorphism

Hmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)≅grk−1W​Hk−1​(𝒦)sign×μ2​(−1).\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})\cong\gr_{k-1}^{W}\mathrm{H}^{k-1}(\mathscr{K})^{\mathrm{sign}\times\mu_{2}}(-1).

The right-hand side of (1.11) is the Hodge realization of a pure motive Mk\Motive_{k} over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} and the Galois representations rk,ℓr_{k,\ell} from (1.6) arise as its ℓ\ell-adic realizations.

That a paper seemingly about LL-functions bears the title “Hodge theory of Kloosterman connections” may come as a surprise. The reason for this choice is that we see Theorem 1.8 as the crux of our contribution. Once we know that all Hodge numbers are either zero or one (equivalently, that the Galois representations rk,ℓr_{k,\ell} are regular), a recent theorem of Patrikis and Taylor [44], building on previous work of Barnet-Lamb, Gee, Geraghty, and Taylor [3], implies that the rk,ℓr_{k,\ell} are potentially automorphic, and hence that their LL-functions meromorphically extend to the complex plane and satisfy a functional equation. As expounded in the sequel paper [20], our approach also explains the relation, numerically checked to high precision by Broadhurst and Roberts in many examples, between special values of the LL-functions at critical integers and certain determinants of Bessel moments

∫0∞I0​(z)a​K0​(z)k−a​zb​𝑑z/z,\int_{0}^{\infty}I_{0}(z)^{a}K_{0}(z)^{k-a}z^{b}{dz}/{z},

where I0​(z)I_{0}(z) and K0​(z)K_{0}(z) are the modified Bessel functions of the first and the second kind.

1.4. Overview

Briefly, the paper is organized as follows. In the preparatory Section 2, we gather the main properties of Kloosterman connections and their symmetric powers. The mixed Hodge structures are constructed in Section 3, where we also exhibit their avatars over finite fields. Section 4 is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.8. Finally, in Section 5 we compute the étale realizations of the motives and pull everything together to prove Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. The paper is supplemented by an appendix concerning exponential mixed Hodge structures and the irregular Hodge filtration.

2. Symmetric powers of Kloosterman connections

In this section, we gather the properties of Kloosterman connections and their symmetric powers that are relevant for the construction of the mixed Hodge structures in the next sections. We refer the reader to Appendix A.1 for the notation and results from the theories of 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules and mixed Hodge modules that are used in what follows, and to [32, §II] for the notion of slopes of a meromorphic connection at an irregular singularity.

    Let Kln+1∨\Kl_{n+1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\vee} be the 𝒪𝔾m\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}-module dual to Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} endowed with the dual connection, and let ιr\iota_{r} denote the involution z↦(−1)r​zz\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}(-1)^{r}z.     Kln+1∨≃ιn+1+​Kln+1.\Kl_{n+1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\vee}\simeq\iota_{n+1}^{+}\Kl_{n+1}.

Proof.

The arguments of [9, Th. 7.4 & 7.8] can readily be transposed to the complex setting to show that Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} is a free 𝒪𝔾m\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}-module with connection sitting in degree zero. Instead, we give a proof based on the following recursive description. Let inv\inv be the involution z↦1/zz\mathchoice{\longmapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}{\mapsto}1/z on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} and consider the localized Fourier transformation

ℱ=j0+​FT⁡j0+:𝖣holb​(𝒟𝔾m)⟶𝖣holb​(𝒟𝔾m).\mathscr{F}=j_{0}^{+}\FT j_{0+}\colon\mathsf{D}^{\mathrm{b}}_{\mathrm{hol}}(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{D}^{\mathrm{b}}_{\mathrm{hol}}(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}).

Recall that this functor preserves holonomic modules, and sends regular holonomic modules to smooth holonomic modules on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} with a regular singularity at the origin and a possibly irregular singularity with slopes in {0,1}\{0,1\} at infinity. For the sake of the induction, it will be convenient to set Kl1=j0+​Ey\Kl_{1}=j_{0}^{+}E^{y} and start with n=0n=0.

Lemma 2.5.

For n⩾0n\geqslant 0, the isomorphism Kln+2≃ℱ​inv+​Kln+1\Kl_{n+2}\simeq\mathscr{F}\inv^{+}\Kl_{n+1} holds.

Proof.

We set z′=1/zz^{\prime}=1/z and x0=z/x1⋯xnx_{0}=z/x_{1}\cdots x_{n}, so that pz′=1/x0⋯xnp_{z^{\prime}}=1/x_{0}\cdots x_{n} and

inv+⁡Kln+1=pz′+​Ex0+⋯+xn.\inv^{+}\Kl_{n+1}=p_{z^{\prime}+}E^{x_{0}+\cdots+x_{n}}.

Hence, denoting by ζ\zeta a coordinate on a new factor 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} and by πζ\pi_{\zeta} the corresponding projection,

ℱinv+Kln+1=πζ+Ex0+⋯+xn+ζ​z′=πζ+Ex0+⋯+xn+ζ/x0⋯xn≃Kln+2.∎\mathscr{F}\inv^{+}\Kl_{n+1}=\pi_{\zeta+}E^{x_{0}+\cdots+x_{n}+\zeta z^{\prime}}=\pi_{\zeta+}E^{x_{0}+\cdots+x_{n}+\zeta/x_{0}\cdots x_{n}}\simeq\Kl_{n+2}.\qed

Let us now show (1) and (2). Since Kl1\Kl_{1} is a holonomic 𝒟𝔾m\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}-module, the same goes for each Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} by induction. That Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} is isomorphic to the free 𝒪𝔾m\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}-module of rank n+1n+1 with connection defined by L=(z∂z)n+1−zL=(z\partial_{z})^{n+1}-z is clear for n=0n=0. Assuming it true for Kln+1\Kl_{n+1}, Lemma 2.5 implies that Kln+2\Kl_{n+2} is isomorphic to

ℱinv+(𝒟𝔾m/𝒟𝔾mL)≃ℱ(𝒟𝔾m/𝒟𝔾m((−z∂z)n+1z−1)))≃𝒟𝔾m/𝒟𝔾m((z∂z)n+2−z),\displaystyle\mathscr{F}\inv^{+}\bigl(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}/\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}L\bigr)\simeq\mathscr{F}\bigl(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}/\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}((-z\partial_{z})^{n+1}z-1))\bigr)\simeq\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}/\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}((z\partial_{z})^{n+2}-z),

where the first isomorphism is given by inversion and multiplication by zz on the right. With respect to a suitable basis, the matrix of z∂zz\partial_{z} acting on Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} is thus given by

(00⋯0z10⋯0001⋯0000⋯10),\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\cdots&0&z\\ 1&0&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&1&\cdots&0&0\\ 0&0&\cdots&1&0\end{pmatrix},

which shows that z=0z=0 is a regular singularity with unipotent monodromy and a single Jordan block. It also follows from this description that z=∞z=\infty is an irregular singularity of slope 1/(n+1){1}/{(n+1)}, and that Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} is irreducible. Indeed, j0+​inv+​Kln+1j_{0+}\inv^{+}\Kl_{n+1} agrees with the intermediate extension j0†+inv+Kln+1j_{0{\dagger}+}\inv^{+}\Kl_{n+1} since inv+⁡Kln+1\inv^{+}\Kl_{n+1} has slope 1/(n+1){1}/{(n+1)} at 00; it is thus an irreducible 𝒟𝔸1\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-module, and Fourier transformation preserves this property.

We note that property (3) is true for n=0n=0. Assuming it holds for Kln+1\Kl_{n+1}, we prove it for Kln+2\Kl_{n+2}. Fourier transformation commutes with duality of 𝒟𝔸1\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-modules up to ι1\iota_{1}, as follows from [40, Lem. V.3.6], and the latter duality corresponds to the duality of free 𝒪𝔾m\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}-modules with connection through the pair of functors j0+j_{0}^{+} and j0†+j_{0{{\dagger}+}}. Thus Lemma 2.5 yields (3).

Finally, the pullback Kl~n+1{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{n+1} of Kln+1\Kl_{n+1} by the finite morphism [n+1][n+1] is also concentrated in degree zero and is smooth of rank n+1n+1 on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}. Consider the 𝒟𝔸1\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-module

Mn+1=ℋ0​g+​𝒪𝔾mn.M_{n+1}=\mathscr{H}^{0}g_{+}\mathscr{O}_{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{n}}.

of 𝐂[t,t−1]⟨t∂t⟩\mathbf{C}[t,t^{-1}]\langle t\partial_{t}\rangle-modules. This will yield (4). Indeed, letting pt:𝔾m,t×𝔸1τ→𝔾m,tp_{t}\colon{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}_{,t}\times\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}_{,t} and pτ:𝔾m,t×𝔸1τ→𝔸1τp_{\tau}\colon{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}_{,t}\times\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau} denote the projections and writing π~\widetilde{\pi} as the composition of Id×g:𝔾m,t×𝔾mn→𝔾m,t×𝔸1\id\times g\colon{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}_{,t}\times\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{n}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}_{,t}\times\mathbb{A}^{\!1} and ptp_{t}, the projection formula gives isomorphisms

Proposition 2.7.

Proof.

In what follows, we consider objects acted upon by one of the groups 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} and 𝔖k×μn+1\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1}, and we use the uniform notation χ:G→{±1}\chi\colon G\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\{\pm 1\} for the sign character if G=𝔖kG=\mathfrak{S}_{k} and the product of the sign character on 𝔖k\mathfrak{S}_{k} and the trivial character on μn+1\mu_{n+1} if G=𝔖k×μn+1G=\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1}. Proposition 2.13.

The de Rham cohomology of Symk⁡Kln+1\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1} and SymkKl~n+1\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{n+1} is concentrated in degree one. Moreover, there are isomorphisms

≃HdR,ck​n+1​(𝔾mk​n+1,Ef~k)𝔖k×μn+1,χn,\displaystyle\simeq\mathrm{H}^{kn+1}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1},E^{\widetilde{f}_{k}})^{\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1},\chi_{n}},

after inverting ∂τ\partial_{\tau}, are isomorphisms. We finally obtain a morphism

inducing an isomorphism after inverting ∂τ\partial_{\tau}, a property which implies the isomorphisms

Lemma 2.24.

The 𝒟𝔸1\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-module M~\widetilde{M} is irreducible and is equal to the image of (2.22).

Proof.

Since SymkKl~n+1\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{n+1} is irreducible by Proposition 2.7, so are j0†+SymkKl~n+1j_{0{{\dagger}+}}\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{n+1} and its inverse Fourier transform M~\widetilde{M}. Besides, the left-hand side M~0\widetilde{M}_{0} of (2.22) underlies a pure Hodge module M~0H\widetilde{M}_{0}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} on the affine line, which decomposes as a direct sum M~1H⊕M~2H\widetilde{M}_{1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\oplus\widetilde{M}_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} in which the 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module M~1\widetilde{M}_{1} underlying M~1H\widetilde{M}_{1}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} is the maximal constant submodule of M~0\widetilde{M}_{0}. The image of (2.22) is thus isomorphic to the 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module M~2\widetilde{M}_{2} underlying M~2H\widetilde{M}_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}. Since M~2H\widetilde{M}_{2}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} is pure, M~2\widetilde{M}_{2} is a direct sum of irreducible 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules, and hence FT⁡(M~2)\FT(\widetilde{M}_{2}) as well. On the other hand, (2.23) gives the equality j0+FT(M~2)=SymkKl~n+1j_{0}^{+}\FT(\widetilde{M}_{2})=\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{n+1}, from which we get FT(M~2)=j0†+SymkKl~=n+1FT(M~)\FT(\widetilde{M}_{2})=j_{0{\dagger}+}\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{n+1}=\FT(\widetilde{M}) as we wanted to show. ∎

The χn\chi_{n}-isotypic component (ℋ0g!∗⊞kHp𝐐UH)𝔖k,χn(\mathscr{H}^{0}{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}g^{\boxplus k}_{!*}\,\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\mathbf{Q}}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}_{U})^{\mathfrak{S}_{k},\,\chi_{n}} is a pure object of weight k​nkn of 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}). 3. Motives of symmetric power moments of Kloosterman connections

The main goal of this section is to prove that the middle de Rham cohomology of the connection Symk⁡Kln+1\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1} is the de Rham realization of a Nori motive over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} (see [28]). The expressions of the various cohomology spaces obtained in Section 2.2 naturally exhibit them as the de Rham fibers of certain exponential mixed Hodge structures, and we begin by showing in Theorem 3.2 that they are in fact usual mixed Hodge structures. Building on this result, we then obtain in Theorem 3.8 a geometric description of the middle mixed Hodge structure in terms of a hypersurface 𝒦⊂𝔾mk​n\mathscr{K}\subset\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn} acted upon by the group 𝔖k×μn+1\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1}. This leads us to define the middle motive Mk\Motive_{k} of Symk⁡Kln+1\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1} as

(3.1) Mk=grk​n+1W​[Hck​n−1​(𝒦)​(−1)]𝔖k×μn+1,χn,\Motive_{k}=\gr^{W}_{kn+1}[\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{c}}^{kn-1}(\mathscr{K})(-1)]^{\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1},\chi_{n}},

where in the right-hand side W∙W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet} stands for the weight filtration, which exists at the motivic level by [28, Th. 10.2.5]. In the second part, we establish the counterpart of these results for the étale cohomology of symmetric powers of the ℓ\ell-adic Kloosterman sheaf and the rigid cohomology of symmetric powers of the Kloosterman FF-isocrystal on 𝔾m\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}} over a finite field. They turn out to be easier to prove because a full formalism of weights is at hand regardless of the ramification of the coefficients, whereas in the Hodge setting we need to resort the interpretation of Symk⁡Kln+1\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1} as the localized Fourier transform of a mixed Hodge module in order to remain within the framework of exponential mixed Hodge structures.

3.1. The mixed Hodge structures attached to Symk⁡Kln+1\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}

Throughout this section, we work in the abelian category 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS of exponential mixed Hodge structures, which is a full subcategory of the category of mixed Hodge modules over the affine line 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1} (see Section A.3 for a review). It contains the category of mixed Hodge structure as a full subcategory (Lemma A.12) and objects Hr​(U,f),\mathrm{H}^{r}(U,f), Hcr​(U,f),\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{c}}^{r}(U,f), and Hmidr​(U,f)\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{mid}}^{r}(U,f) associated with a regular function f:U→𝔸1f\colon U\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} and an integer rr, whose de Rham fibers are the cohomology spaces HdRr​(U,Ef),\mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{dR}}^{r}(U,E^{f}), HdR,cr​(U,Ef),\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}^{r}(U,E^{f}), and HdR,midr​(U,Ef)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}^{r}(U,E^{f}) respectively (see Section A.5).

Recall from (2.8) the Laurent polynomial fkf_{k} on the torus 𝔾mk​n+1\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1} with coordinates (z,xj​i)(z,x_{ji}) and its pullback f~k\widetilde{f}_{k} to the torus 𝔾mk​n+1\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1} with coordinates (t,xj​i)(t,x_{ji}) by the map z↦tn+1z\mapsto t^{n+1}. The group 𝔖k×μn+1\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1} acts on 𝔾mk​n+1=𝔾m,t×(𝔾mn)k\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1}={\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}}_{,t}\times(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{n})^{k} by permutation of the copies of 𝔾mn\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{n} and multiplication on the coordinate tt. As this action leaves f~k\widetilde{f}_{k} invariant, the objects Hk​n+1​(𝔾mk​n+1,f~k)\mathrm{H}^{kn+1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1},\widetilde{f}_{k}) and Hck​n+1​(𝔾mk​n+1,f~k)\mathrm{H}^{kn+1}_{{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1},\widetilde{f}_{k}) of the category 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS inherit an action of 𝔖k×μn+1\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1}.

For ?=∅,c,mid?=\varnothing,{\mathrm{c}},{\mathrm{mid}}, we define the objects

H?1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1)\displaystyle\mathrm{H}_{?}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}) =H?k​n+1​(𝔾mk​n+1,fk)𝔖k,χn=H?k​n+1​(𝔾mk​n+1,f~k)𝔖k×μn+1,χn,\displaystyle=\mathrm{H}_{?}^{kn+1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1},f_{k})^{\mathfrak{S}_{k},\,\chi_{n}}=\mathrm{H}_{?}^{kn+1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{kn+1},\widetilde{f}_{k})^{\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{n+1},\,\chi_{n}},

of the category 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS, the de Rham fibers of which are nothing but HdR,?1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},?}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}) and HdR,?1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl~n+1)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},?}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\widetilde{\Kl}_{n+1}) in view of Proposition 2.13 and Corollary 2.15.

Theorem 3.2.

The exponential mixed Hodge structures

H1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1),Hc1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1),andHmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}),\quad\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}),\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1})

are usual mixed Hodge structures of weights ⩾k​n+1\geqslant kn+1, ⩽k​n+1\leqslant kn+1, and k​n+1kn+1 respectively, and the natural morphisms between them are morphisms of mixed Hodge structures.

Moreover, the induced map

Proof.

Once we know that Hc1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{c}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}) and H1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1)\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}) are both mixed Hodge structures, the natural morphism between them is a morphism of Hodge structures since 𝖬𝖧𝖲\MHS is a full subcategory of 𝖤𝖬𝖧𝖲\EMHS by Lemma A.12. Its image Hmid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kln+1)\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1}) is therefore a usual mixed Hodge structure as well. Remark 3.10.

The hypersurface 𝒦\mathscr{K} has at worst isolated singularities, its 𝐐¯\overline{\mathbf{Q}}-singular points being those with coordinates yj​i=ζjy_{ji}=\zeta_{j} for all 1⩽j⩽k1\leqslant j\leqslant k and 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n, where ζj∈μn+1\zeta_{j}\in\mu_{n+1} are roots of unity satisfying ∑j=1kζj=0\sum_{j=1}^{k}\zeta_{j}=0. (This is reminiscent of the computation of the Swan conductor at infinity of the analogue of Symk⁡Kln+1\Sym^{k}\Kl_{n+1} over finite fields in [21, Th. 3.1].) For example, if n+1n+1 is a prime number, then 𝒦\mathscr{K} is singular if and only if kk is a multiple of n+1n+1; this includes the case n=1n=1, in which 𝒦\mathscr{K} is singular if and only if kk is even.

3.2. The case of characteristic pp

In this section, we prove an analogue of Theorem 3.8 for the étale and rigid cohomology of symmetric powers of Kloosterman sheaves over finite fields.

4. Computation of the Hodge filtration

From now on, we focus on the case n=1n=1. In this section, we construct a basis of the de Rham cohomology of the symmetric power Symk⁡Kl2\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2} that is well enough behaved with respect to the Hodge filtration for us to be able to prove Theorem 1.8 from the introduction.

Statement (1) follows from 4.6(3). For (2), the question is local analytic around the point z=0z=0. 4.3. The Hodge filtration

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.8. In order to do so, we first establish the analogue of this result for SymkKl~2\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{2}, which is stated as follows:

    For even kk, it is mixed of weights k+1k+1, k+2k+2 and 2​k+22k+\penalty 2, with

    dimH1(𝔾m,SymkKl~)2p,q={1,p+q=k+1,p∈{1,…,k} and p≠k/2,k/2+1,1,p=q=k/2+1,1,p=q=k+1,0,otherwise.\dim\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{2})^{p,q}=\begin{cases}1,&p+q=k+1,\;p\in\{1,\dots,k\}\text{ and }p\neq k/2,\,k/2+1,\\ 1,&p=q=k/2+1,\\ 1,&p=q=k+1,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The weight properties of H1(𝔾m,SymkKl~)2\mathrm{H}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{2}) and the purity of Hmid1(𝔾m,SymkKl~)2\mathrm{H}^{1}_{{\mathrm{mid}}}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}{\widetilde{\Kl}}{}_{2}) were already obtained in the more general setting of Theorem 3.2. To compute the Hodge numbers, we take up the argument in its proof for n=1n=1. 5. LL-functions

In this section, we compute the LL-function of the pure motive Mk\Motive_{k} over 𝐐\mathbf{Q} defined in (3.1). We first compare, in Theorems 5.8 and 5.18, the traces of Frobenius at unramified primes of its ℓ\ell-adic realization with symmetric power moments of Kloosterman sums. These results largely overlap with Yun’s [64, Th. 1.1.6]. Up to semi-simplification, the two approaches yield the same Galois representations as realizations of two different geometric models. In some sense, we have replaced the use of affine Grassmannians and homogeneous Fourier transformation in [64] with that of exponential mixed Hodge structures and the irregular Hodge filtration to obtain the easier geometric model 𝒦\mathscr{K} in terms of which the motive is defined (compare with [64, §4.1.6]). One advantage of this point of view is that it enables us to determine the structure of the Galois representations at ramified primes by means of the Picard-Lefschetz formula. In addition, we show in Proposition 5.26 that the Galois representations are crystalline at p>kp>k when kk is odd (resp. p>k/2p>{k}/{2} when kk is even) and we obtain lower bounds for the pp-adic valuation of the eigenvalues of Frobenius in Corollary 5.30. We then compute the gamma factor in Corollary 5.33. Using the Patrikis-Taylor theorem, we finally prove that the motives (3.1) are potentially automorphic in the last subsection. Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 from the introduction follow by pulling everything together.

5.1. Étale realizations

5.1.2. Galois representations of symmetric power moments

Recall from (3.9) the Laurent polynomial g⊞k=∑i=1k(yi+1/yi)g^{\boxplus k}=\sum_{i=1}^{k}(y_{i}+{1}/{y_{i}}) on the torus 𝔾mk\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k} and its zero locus 𝒦⊂𝔾mk\mathscr{K}\subset\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k}. For each prime number ℓ\ell, the ℓ\ell-adic realization of the motive Mk\Motive_{k} is the 𝐐ℓ\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}-vector space

(5.5) Vk,ℓ=grk−1W​Hét,ck−1​(𝒦𝐐¯,𝐐ℓ)𝔖k×μ2,χ​(−1)V_{k,\ell}=\gr^{W}_{k-1}\mathrm{H}_{\textup{\'{e}t},{\mathrm{c}}}^{k-1}(\mathscr{K}_{\overline{\mathbf{Q}}},\mathbf{Q}_{\ell})^{\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{2},\,\chi}(-1)

equipped with the continuous representation

Writing k=2​m+1k=2m+1 for odd kk and k=2​m+2k=2m+2 or k=2​m+4k=2m+4 with mm an even integer for even kk, the vector space Vk,ℓV_{k,\ell} is mm-dimensional by (4.15).

The goal of the next two sections is to compare the traces of Frobenius at unramified primes with symmetric power moments of Kloosterman sums. For this, we shall consider the toric compactification XX of 𝔾mk\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k} introduced in Section 4.3.2 and let 𝒦¯\overline{\mathscr{K}} be the closure of 𝒦\mathscr{K} in XX. We also regard these varieties as defined over general rings (e.g. over 𝐅p,𝐙p\mathbf{F}_{p},\mathbf{Z}_{p}, etc.). We claim that 𝒦¯\overline{\mathscr{K}} is smooth along the strict normal crossing divisor D=X∖𝔾mkD=X\smallsetminus\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k} and that each irreducible component of DD intersects 𝒦¯\overline{\mathscr{K}} in a smooth divisor in such a way that 𝒦¯∖𝒦\overline{\mathscr{K}}\smallsetminus\mathscr{K} forms a relative strict normal crossing divisor over 𝐙\mathbf{Z}. Indeed, it is enough to check these properties on each of the 2k​k!2^{k}k! affine charts of XX corresponding to the cones of maximal dimension of the simplicial fan FF. For example, on the chart X1≅𝔸k=Spec⁡(𝐙​[zi]i=1k)X_{1}\cong\mathbb{A}^{k}=\Spec(\mathbf{Z}[z_{i}]_{i=1}^{k}), the function g⊞kg^{\boxplus k} is given by g⊞k=g1/z1⋯zkg^{\boxplus k}={g_{1}}/{z_{1}\cdots z_{k}} and the equality 𝒦¯∩X1=(g1)\overline{\mathscr{K}}\cap X_{1}=(g_{1}) holds, with g1g_{1} as in (4.28). One then checks the equalities

(g1)∩(z1)\displaystyle(g_{1})\cap(z_{1}) =∅,(g1)∩(zr)=(1+z1(1+z2+⋯+z2⋯zr−1))\displaystyle=\varnothing,\quad(g_{1})\cap(z_{r})=\bigl(1+z_{1}(1+z_{2}+\cdots+z_{2}\cdots z_{r-1})\bigr)
(∂g1/∂z1)∩(zr)=(1+z2+⋯+z2⋯zr−1)\displaystyle(\partial g_{1}/\partial z_{1})\cap(z_{r})=\bigl(1+z_{2}+\cdots+z_{2}\cdots z_{r-1}\bigr)

for r=2,…,kr=2,\dots,k. From the first two, it follows that ∂g1/∂z1\partial g_{1}/\partial z_{1} does not vanish on (zr)(z_{r}) for r⩾2r\geqslant 2, hence the smoothness of 𝒦¯\overline{\mathscr{K}} along (z1⋯zr)(z_{1}\cdots z_{r}). The smoothness of (g1)∩(zr)(g_{1})\cap(z_{r}) is also clear, and 𝒦¯∩(zr1)∩⋯∩(zri)\overline{\mathscr{K}}\cap(z_{r_{1}})\cap\cdots\cap(z_{r_{i}}) is smooth for any sequence 2⩽r1⩽⋯⩽ri⩽k2\leqslant r_{1}\leqslant\cdots\leqslant r_{i}\leqslant k, which implies the strict normal crossing property. Besides, over 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, the variety 𝒦⊂𝔾mk\mathscr{K}\subset\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}}^{k} is smooth when kk is odd, while if kk is even, its singular locus consists of (kk/2)\binom{k}{k/2} ordinary quadratic points with coordinates yi∈{±1}y_{i}\in\{\pm 1\} satisfying ∑i=1kyi=0\sum_{i=1}^{k}y_{i}=0.

5.1.4. The ℓ\ell-adic case for even symmetric powers

Corollary 5.30.

Let k⩾1k\geqslant 1 be an integer and pp an odd prime number. The Newton polygon of the Frobenius module Hrig,c1​(𝔾m,𝐅p/K,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}_{\rig,{\mathrm{c}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\mathbf{F}_{p}}/K,\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) lies above the Hodge polygon of HdR,c1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}). In case p>kp>k if kk is odd or 2​p>k2p>k if kk is even, the endpoints of both polygons coincide.

Proof.

Considered as a representation of Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/𝐐p​(−p))\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/\mathbf{Q}_{p}(\sqrt{-p})), the pp-adic étale realization Vk,pV_{k,p} of Mk\Motive_{k} is semistable, and hence the associated filtered (φ,N)(\varphi,{\mathrm{N}})-module (Vk,p⊗𝐁st)Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/𝐐p​(−p))(V_{k,p}\otimes\!\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{st}})^{\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/\mathbf{Q}_{p}(\sqrt{-p}))} is (weakly) admissible. This means precisely that its Newton polygon lies above its Hodge polygon, both having the same endpoints. Notice that these polygons are additive with respect to the Minkowski sum (i.e., the sum of the convex sets above the polygons in the plane 𝐑2\mathbf{R}^{2}) for filtered Frobenius modules. Since the Frobenius module Hrig,mid1​(𝔾m,𝐅p/K,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}_{\rig,{\mathrm{mid}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m},\mathbf{F}_{p}}/K,\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) injects (after extending scalars to KK) into the Frobenius module associated with Vk,pV_{k,p} by Proposition 5.26, the Newton polygon of the former lies above that of the latter, which in turns lies above the Hodge polygon of HdR,mid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) by admissibility. Moreover, under the condition p>kp>k (resp. p>k/2p>{k}/{2}) if kk is odd (resp. even), the two Frobenius modules are equal by Proposition 5.26, and hence both polygons have the same endpoints. We conclude the proof by putting the trivial factor back, which is one-dimensional with Frobenius and Hodge slopes 00 if k≢0mod4k\not\equiv 0\bmod{4} and two-dimensional with Frobenius and Hodge slopes 00 and k/2{k}/{2} otherwise. ∎

Remark 5.31.

Writing Zk​(p,T)=∑cn​TnZ_{k}(p;T)=\sum c_{n}T^{n}, the above corollary implies in particular that the inequality

(5.32) vp​(cn)⩾n⁡(n−1)v_{p}(c_{n})\geqslant n(n-1)

holds for all p⩾3p\geqslant 3. This sharpens a theorem of Haessig [25, Th. 1.1], who obtained the lower bound (1−1/(p−1))​n​(n−1)\left(1-{1}/{(p-1)}\right)n(n-1) for all p⩾5p\geqslant 5 using pp-adic analysis à la Dwork. While this paper was being refereed, he managed to prove (5.32) for all p⩾2p\geqslant 2 by strengthening his previous arguments [26]. As we explain in Remark 5.44 infra, it is also possible to obtain this lower bound in all cases except for p=2p=2 and even kk from the potential automorphy of the motive Mk\Motive_{k}. Note that, when kk is even, the Hodge polygon of HdR,c1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) lies strictly above the polygon with vertices n⁡(n−1)n(n-1), as Figure 1 shows.

5.2. The gamma factor

We first recall Serre’s recipe [57, §3] describing the conjectural shape of the gamma factor at infinity in the complete LL-function of a pure motive over 𝐐\mathbf{Q}. Let VV be a finite-dimensional vector space over 𝐂\mathbf{C} together with an 𝐑\mathbf{R}-Hodge decomposition of weight ww, i.e., the data of a grading V=⨁p∈𝐙VpV=\mathop{\textstyle\bigoplus}\displaylimits_{p\in\mathbf{Z}}V^{p} and a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-linear involution σ\sigma of VV such that σ⁡(Vp)=Vw−p\sigma(V^{p})=V^{w-p}. Given an 𝐑\mathbf{R}-Hodge decomposition, we set h⁡(p)=dim𝐂Vph(p)=\dim_{\mathbf{C}}V^{p} and

h​(w/2)±=dim𝐂{v∈Vw/2|σ⁡(v)=±(−1)w/2​v}h({w}/{2})^{\pm}=\dim_{\mathbf{C}}\left\{v\in V^{w/2}\,|\,\sigma(v)=\pm(-1)^{w/2}v\right\}

if ww is even and h​(w/2)±=0h({w}/{2})^{\pm}=0 otherwise. Setting

5.3. Potential automorphy, meromorphic continuation, and functional equation

In this final section, we pull everything together to prove Theorems 1.2 and 1.3 from the introduction. We first compute the ε\varepsilon-factors of the Galois representations Vk,ℓV_{k,\ell} and recall the particular case of the theorem of Patrikis and Taylor that will imply potential automorphy.

5.3.1. Weil-Deligne representations and ε\varepsilon-factors

For each integer k⩾1k\geqslant 1, consider the system {Vk,ℓ}ℓ\{V_{k,\ell}\}_{\ell} of ℓ\ell-adic realizations of the motive Mk\Motive_{k}. We investigate its global ε\varepsilon-factor εk​(s)\varepsilon_{k}(s) by means of the information obtained in Theorems 5.8 and 5.18. We refer the reader to [60] for an accessible introduction to Weil-Deligne representations.

As inputs for defining the local ε\varepsilon-factor of {Vk,ℓ}\{V_{k,\ell}\} at each place pp of 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, we fix the additive character ψ\psi and the Haar measure d​x{\mathrm{d}}x on 𝐐p\mathbf{Q}_{p} as follows. If p<∞p<\infty, then ψ\psi is the composition

𝐐p⟶𝐐p/𝐙p=𝐙⁡[1/p]/𝐙⟶𝐂×,\mathbf{Q}_{p}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{Q}_{p}/\mathbf{Z}_{p}=\mathbf{Z}[{1}/{p}]/\mathbf{Z}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{C}^{\times},

Letting 𝐀𝐐\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{Q}} denote the adele ring of 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, these local characters and Haar measures are compatible in the sense that the product of the ψ\psi’s induces a character of 𝐀𝐐/𝐐\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q} and the compact quotient 𝐀𝐐/𝐐\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q} has volume 11 with respect to the induced measure [8, §3.10].

of degree (k−2)/2−δ4​𝐙​(k)−⌊k/6⌋,{(k-2)}/{2}-\delta_{4\mathbf{Z}}(k)-\left\lfloor{k}/{6}\right\rfloor, where bkb_{k} and Mk​(2,T)M_{k}(2;T) are defined in (5.4).

5.3.2. The theorem of Patrikis-Taylor

Let m⩾1m\geqslant 1 be an integer and SS a finite set of prime numbers. We consider a weakly compatible system of continuous semi-simple representations

rℓ:Gal⁡(𝐐¯/𝐐)⟶GLm⁡(𝐐¯ℓ)r_{\ell}\colon\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q})\longrightarrow\GL_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell})

with ℓ\ell running over all prime numbers. The notion of being “weakly compatible” is borrowed from [3, 5.1] and means that the following three conditions hold:

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    if p∉Sp\notin S, then for all ℓ≠p\ell\neq p the representation rℓr_{\ell} is unramified at pp and the characteristic polynomial of rℓ​(Frobp)r_{\ell}(\mathrm{Frob}_{p}) lies in 𝐐⁡[T]\mathbf{Q}[T] and is independent of ℓ\ell;

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    each representation rℓr_{\ell} is de Rham and in fact crystalline if ℓ∉S\ell\notin S;

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    the Hodge-Tate weights of rℓr_{\ell} are independent of ℓ\ell.

Theorem 5.41 (Patrikis-Taylor, [44, Th. A]).

Let ℛ={rℓ}\mathscr{R}=\{r_{\ell}\} be a weakly compatible system that satisfies the following three properties:

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    (Purity) There exists an integer ww such that, for each prime p∉Sp\notin S, the roots of the common characteristic polynomial of rℓ​(Frobp)r_{\ell}(\mathrm{Frob}_{p}) are Weil numbers of weight ww.

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    (Regularity) The representation rℓr_{\ell} has mm distinct Hodge-Tate weights.

  • ∙\scriptscriptstyle\bullet

    (Odd essential self-duality) Either each rℓr_{\ell} factors through a map to GOm​(𝐐¯ℓ)\mathrm{GO}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}) with even similitude character or each rℓr_{\ell} factors through a map to GSpm​(𝐐¯ℓ)\mathrm{GSp}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}) with odd similitude character. Moreover, these characters form a weakly compatible system.

Then there exists a finite, Galois, totally real number field over which all of the rℓr_{\ell} become automorphic. In particular, the partial LL-function

LS​(ℛ,s)=∏p∉Sdet(1−rℓ​(Frobp)​p−s)−1L^{S}(\mathscr{R},s)=\prod_{p\notin S}\det(1-r_{\ell}(\mathrm{Frob}_{p})p^{-s})^{-1}

admits a meromorphic continuation to the complex plane.

Let pp and ℓ\ell be distinct prime numbers and let (ρ,N)(\rho,{\mathrm{N}}) be the Weil-Deligne representation on V≃𝐐¯ℓmV\simeq\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}^{m} associated with rℓr_{\ell}. There is a unique increasing monodromy filtration V⩽⁣∙⊂VV^{\leqslant{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}}\subset V attached to the nilpotent endomorphism N{\mathrm{N}} such that the inclusion N​V⩽a⊂V⩽a−2{\mathrm{N}}V^{\leqslant a}\subset V^{\leqslant a-2} holds for each integer aa and that the map V⩽a/V⩽a−1→V⩽−a/V⩽−a−1V^{\leqslant a}/V^{\leqslant a-1}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}V^{\leqslant-a}/V^{\leqslant-a-1} induced by Na{\mathrm{N}}^{a} is an isomorphism for all a⩾0a\geqslant 0. Recall that (ρ,N)(\rho,{\mathrm{N}}) is called pure of weight ww if the eigenvalues of Frobenius FpF_{p} acting on V⩽a/V⩽a−1V^{\leqslant a}/V^{\leqslant a-1} are pp-Weil numbers of weight w+aw+a for all aa. Building on vast work on constructions of Galois representations attached to automorphic representations, which is partly summarized in [3, Th. 2.1.1], Theorem 5.41 implies the following:

Corollary 5.42 ([44, Cor. 2.2 (ii)]).

Let ℛ={rℓ}\mathscr{R}=\{r_{\ell}\} be a weakly compatible system that is pure of weight ww, regular, and odd essential self-dual. Then, for any distinct primes pp and ℓ\ell, the Weil-Deligne representation WDp​(ℛ)\mathrm{WD}_{p}(\mathscr{R}) of Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/𝐐p)\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/\mathbf{Q}_{p}) associated with rℓr_{\ell} is pure of weight ww. Moreover, with the notation of [3, 5.1], the completed LL-function

Λ⁡(ℛ,s)=L∞​(ℛ,s)⋅∏p∈SL⁡(WDp​(ℛ),s)⋅LS​(ℛ,s)\Lambda(\mathscr{R},s)=L_{\infty}(\mathscr{R},s)\cdot\prod_{p\in S}L(\mathrm{WD}_{p}(\mathscr{R}),s)\cdot L^{S}(\mathscr{R},s)

satisfies the functional equation Λ⁡(ℛ,s)=ε⁡(ℛ,s)​Λ​(ℛ∨,1−s)\Lambda(\mathscr{R},s)=\varepsilon(\mathscr{R},s)\Lambda(\mathscr{R}^{\scriptscriptstyle\vee},1-s).

5.3.3. Proof of Theorems 1.2 and 1.3

For each integer k⩾1k\geqslant 1, the ℓ\ell-adic representations

are pure of weight k+1k+1. After choosing an embedding 𝐐p↪𝐂\mathbf{Q}_{p}\hookrightarrow\mathbf{C}, we get a filtered isomorphism

=grk−1W​HdR,ck−1​(𝒦𝐐p)𝔖k×μ2,χ​(−1)⊗𝐂\displaystyle=\gr^{W}_{k-1}\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{c}}}^{k-1}(\mathscr{K}_{\mathbf{Q}_{p}})^{\mathfrak{S}_{k}\times\mu_{2},\chi}(-1)\otimes\mathbf{C}
≅HdR,mid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\displaystyle\cong\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2})

by the pp-adic comparison theorem. By definition, the Hodge-Tate weights of Vk,pV_{k,p} are those integers aa such that the graded piece grFa​HdR,mid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\gr_{F}^{a}\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}) is non-zero, counted with multiplicity its dimension. As the Hodge numbers are either 00 or 11 by Theorem 1.8, the system {rk,ℓ}\{r_{k,\ell}\} is regular. Besides, the existence of the (−1)k+1(-1)^{k+1}-symmetric perfect pairing (3.4) implies that the rk,ℓr_{k,\ell} factor through GOm​(𝐐¯ℓ)\mathrm{GO}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}) (resp. GSpm​(𝐐¯ℓ)\mathrm{GSp}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell})) if kk is odd (resp. even) with similitude character χcyc−k−1\chi_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{-k-1}. Choose a basis of 𝐐ℓ​(−k−1)\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}(-k-1) and regard the perfect pairing Vk,ℓ×Vk,ℓ→𝐐ℓ​(−k−1)V_{k,\ell}\times V_{k,\ell}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}(-k-1) as a compatible non-degenerate bilinear form on the module Vk,ℓV_{k,\ell} over the group ring 𝐐ℓ​[Gal⁡(𝐐¯/𝐐)]\mathbf{Q}_{\ell}[\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}/\mathbf{Q})] with the involution g↦χcyc−k−1​(g)​g−1g\mapsto\chi_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{-k-1}(g)g^{-1}. By [58, Th. 4.2.1], the semi-simplification rk,ℓssr_{k,\ell}^{\mathrm{ss}} also factors through GOm​(𝐐¯ℓ)\mathrm{GO}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell}) (resp. GSpm​(𝐐¯ℓ)\mathrm{GSp}_{m}(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\ell})) with similitude character χcyc−k−1\chi_{\mathrm{cyc}}^{-k-1}. Moreover, rk,ℓssr_{k,\ell}^{\mathrm{ss}} is de Rham at all primes ℓ\ell and crystalline if ℓ>k\ell>k by Proposition 5.26. Therefore, the rk,ℓssr_{k,\ell}^{\mathrm{ss}} form a weakly compatible system satisfying the assumptions of the theorem of Patrikis and Taylor and the partial LL-function of {rk,ℓss}\{r_{k,\ell}^{\mathrm{ss}}\} has meromorphic continuation and satisfies the expected automorphic functional equation.

We now show that the LL-function and the ε\varepsilon-factor of {rk,ℓss}\{r_{k,\ell}^{\mathrm{ss}}\} coincide with those of {rk,ℓ}\{r_{k,\ell}\}. For odd kk, this was the content of Remarks 5.16 and 5.38. For even kk, we rely on the following lemma, which is certainly well-known to experts. (We thank one of the referees for suggesting the statement and sketching a proof, which we include for lack of an appropriate reference.)

Lemma 5.43.

Let pp and ℓ\ell be distinct prime numbers, and r:Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/𝐐p)→GL⁡(V)r\colon\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/\mathbf{Q}_{p})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\GL(V) an ℓ\ell-adic representation. Suppose that there exists a sequence

0=V0⊂V1⊂⋯⊂Vc=V0=V_{0}\subset V_{1}\subset\cdots\subset V_{c}=V

of Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/𝐐p)\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/\mathbf{Q}_{p})-stable subspaces such that the Weil-Deligne representation associated with the induced representation r¯\bar{r} on V¯=⨁i=1cVi/Vi−1\overline{V}=\mathop{\textstyle\bigoplus}\displaylimits_{i=1}^{c}V_{i}/V_{i-1} is pure. Then the Weil-Deligne representation associated with rr is pure as well, and rr and r¯\bar{r} have the same LL and ε\varepsilon-factors.

Proof.

Let (ρ,N)(\rho,{\mathrm{N}}) and (ρ¯,N¯)(\bar{\rho},\overline{{\mathrm{N}}}) be the Weil-Deligne representations associated with rr and r¯\bar{r}. By its defining properties (see [8, Th.4.1(1)]), the factor ε0​(ρ,s)\varepsilon_{0}(\rho,s) in (5.36) only depends on the semi-simplification of rr. Set φ=ρ⁡(Fp)\varphi=\rho(F_{p}). It follows from the relation N​φ=p​φ​N{\mathrm{N}}\varphi=p\varphi{\mathrm{N}} that, if α\alpha is an eigenvalue of φ\varphi acting on V⩽a/V⩽a−1V^{\leqslant a}/V^{\leqslant a-1} with multiplicity μ\mu, then α​p−b\alpha p^{-b} is an eigenvalue of φ\varphi acting on V⩽a−2​b/V⩽a−2​b−1V^{\leqslant a-2b}/V^{\leqslant a-2b-1} with multiplicity at least μ\mu for all 0⩽b⩽a0\leqslant b\leqslant a. Besides, by the uniqueness of the monodromy of ℓ\ell-adic representations in Grothendieck’s quasi-unipotency theorem, N{\mathrm{N}} restricts to the logarithm on each ViV_{i}, and hence induces the monodromy N¯\overline{{\mathrm{N}}} on V¯\overline{V}. Since (ρ¯,N¯)(\bar{\rho},\overline{{\mathrm{N}}}) is pure and det(1−φ​T)=det(1−φ¯​T)\det(1-\varphi T)=\det(1-\bar{\varphi}T), we conclude that the monodromy filtrations on (ρ,N)(\rho,{\mathrm{N}}) and (ρ¯,N¯)(\bar{\rho},\overline{{\mathrm{N}}}) have the same dimension on each graded piece and that (ρ,N)(\rho,{\mathrm{N}}) is pure as well. In addition, the two Weil representations ρ|ker⁡(N)\rho|_{\ker({\mathrm{N}})} and ρ¯|ker⁡(N¯)\bar{\rho}|_{\ker(\overline{{\mathrm{N}}})} have the same semi-simplification. Finally, observe that taking IpI_{p}-invariants is exact on Weil representations since IpI_{p} acts through finite quotients, hence the identities

det(1−φ​T∣ker⁡(N)ρ⁡(Ip))\displaystyle\det\big(1-\varphi T\mid\ker({\mathrm{N}})^{\rho(I_{p})}\big) =det(1−φ¯​T∣ker⁡(N¯)ρ¯​(Ip)),\displaystyle=\det\big(1-\bar{\varphi}T\mid\ker(\overline{{\mathrm{N}}})^{\bar{\rho}(I_{p})}\big),
det(φ​T∣Vρ⁡(Ip)/ker⁡(N)ρ⁡(Ip))\displaystyle\det\big(\varphi T\mid V^{\rho(I_{p})}/\ker({\mathrm{N}})^{\rho(I_{p})}\big) =det(φ¯​T∣V¯ρ¯​(Ip)/ker⁡(N¯)ρ¯​(Ip)),\displaystyle=\det\big(\bar{\varphi}T\mid\overline{V}^{\bar{\rho}(I_{p})}/\ker(\overline{{\mathrm{N}}})^{\bar{\rho}(I_{p})}\big),

from which the equality of the LL and the ε\varepsilon-factors follows. ∎

The discussion of paragraph 5.3.1 supra then implies that this functional equation is, up to sign, precisely the one from Theorems 1.2 and 1.3. To conclude, we need to show that the sign is always positive for odd kk; for this we use T. Saito’s result [55] that the sign of the functional equation of the LL-function of an orthogonal motive of even weight is always positive. ∎

Remark 5.44.

As explained in [44, Cor. 2.2 (ii)], another consequence of the potential automorphy of the weakly compatible system {rk,ℓ}ℓ\{r_{k,\ell}\}_{\ell} is that it is indeed strictly compatible (see [44, p. 214] for this notion). Given a prime pp, this allows one to transfer some properties of the ℓ\ell-adic representations rk,ℓr_{k,\ell} for ℓ≠p\ell\neq p, to the pp-adic representation rk,pr_{k,p} of Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/𝐐p)\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/\mathbf{Q}_{p}), since their associated Weil-Deligne representations ρk,ℓ\rho_{k,\ell} and ρk,p\rho_{k,p} are isomorphic up to semi-simplification. (See e.g., [60, §1] for the construction of the Weil-Deligne representation associated with a pp-adic de Rham representation.) In particular, the representation rk,pr_{k,p} is semistable over L=𝐐pL=\mathbf{Q}_{p} if kk is even and L=𝐐p​(−p)L=\mathbf{Q}_{p}(\sqrt{-p}) if kk is odd since ρk,ℓ​(IL)={1}\rho_{k,\ell}(I_{L})=\{1\}, where IL⊂Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/L)I_{L}\subset\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/L) denotes the inertia group (see Section 5.3.1). Moreover, if kk is odd, then N=0{\mathrm{N}}=0, and hence rk,pr_{k,p} is indeed crystalline over LL. This strengthens the statement of Proposition 5.26, where semi-stability was only proved over 𝐐p​(−p)\mathbf{Q}_{p}(\sqrt{-p}). Besides, we have shown in (5.14) and (5.24) that the polynomial Mk​(p,T)M_{k}(p;T) is a factor of det(1−Fp​T∣Vk,ℓIp)\det(1-F_{p}T\mid V_{k,\ell}^{I_{p}}) for all primes pp if kk is odd and for all primes p≠2p\neq 2 if kk is even. From the (weak) admissibility of rk,pr_{k,p} and the equalities

det(1−Fp​T∣Vk,ℓIp)=det(1−Fp​T∣ker⁡(N)ρ⁡(Ip))=det(1−φ​T∣(Vk,p⊗𝐁st)Gal⁡(𝐐¯p/L)),\det\big(1-F_{p}T\mid V_{k,\ell}^{I_{p}}\big)=\det\big(1-F_{p}T\mid\ker({\mathrm{N}})^{\rho(I_{p})}\big)=\det\big(1-\varphi T\mid(V_{k,p}\otimes\mathbf{B}_{\mathrm{st}})^{\Gal(\overline{\mathbf{Q}}_{p}/L)}\big),

it follows that the pp-adic Newton polygon of Mk​(p,T)M_{k}(p;T) lies above the Hodge polygon of HdR,mid1​(𝔾m,Symk⁡Kl2)\mathrm{H}_{{\mathrm{dR}},{\mathrm{mid}}}^{1}(\mathbb{G}_{\mathrm{m}},\Sym^{k}\Kl_{2}). We then recover Corollary 5.30 by adding back the trivial factor, including additionally the case of p=2p=2 and odd kk, which was not treated in loc. cit.

Appendix. Exponential mixed Hodge structures and
irregular Hodge filtrations

In this appendix, we prove some of the theorems used in the main text concerning mixed Hodge structures obtained from exponential mixed Hodge structures. We start by recalling the necessary material on 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules, mixed Hodge modules, and exponential mixed Hodge modules. Proposition A.13 then provides us with a condition for getting a mixed Hodge structure from the irregular Hodge filtration, and a criterion for this condition to be satisfied is proved in Theorem A.26. Finally, Theorem A.32 gives a way to compute the corresponding Hodge and weight filtrations. As it is customary, we adopt the convention that filtrations with lower (resp. upper) indices are increasing (resp. decreasing), and we pass from increasing to decreasing filtrations by setting Firrp=F−pirrF_{\mathrm{irr}}^{p}=F^{\mathrm{irr}}_{-p} for any p∈𝐐p\in\mathbf{Q}, and similarly for the ordinary Hodge filtration. In the theory of mixed Hodge modules one usually considers increasing filtrations, while the Hodge filtration of mixed Hodge structures is usually decreasing. We will make use of both conventions without further explanation.

A.1. Notation and results from the theory of 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules

We refer the reader e.g. to [27, 31] for this section, although the notation therein may be somewhat different.

Given an algebraic morphism h:X→Yh\colon X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}Y between smooth complex algebraic varieties, we denote by h+h_{+} (resp. h+h^{+}) the derived pushforward (resp. pullback) in the sense of 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules; that is, for a 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module or a bounded complex of 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-modules (resp. 𝒟Y\mathscr{D}_{Y}-modules) MM, we set

h+​M=R​h∗​(𝒟Y←X​⊗L𝒟X​M)(resp.​h+​M=𝒟X→Y​⊗Lh−1​𝒟Y​h−1​M).h_{+}M=\mathrm{R}h_{*}\Bigl(\mathscr{D}_{Y\leftarrow X}\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{\mathscr{D}_{X}}M\Bigr)\quad(\text{resp.}\kern 3.00003pth^{+}M=\mathscr{D}_{X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}Y}\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}_{h^{-1}\mathscr{D}_{Y}}h^{-1}M).

We denote by DR⁡M\DR M the analytic de Rham complex of MM, with ManM^{\mathrm{an}} sitting in degree zero, and by p​DR⁡M\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M the shifted complex DR⁡M⁡[dimX]\DR M[\dim X], which is a perverse sheaf. We also denote by h†h_{\dagger} the adjoint by duality of h+h_{+} (that is, the functor h†=𝑫Y​h+​𝑫Xh_{\dagger}=\boldsymbol{D}_{Y}h_{+}\boldsymbol{D}_{X}, where 𝑫\boldsymbol{D} denotes the duality functor in the category of 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules), so that there is a natural morphism h†​M→h+​Mh_{\dagger}M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}h_{+}M. In particular, given a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module MM with regular singularities at infinity, the morphism h†​M→h+​Mh_{\dagger}M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}h_{+}M induces the natural morphism Rh!pDRM→Rh∗pDRM\mathrm{R}h_{!}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathrm{R}h_{*}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M upon application of the shifted de Rham functor and taking the isomorphisms p​DR⁡h+​M≃R​h∗​p​DR⁡M\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}h_{+}M\simeq\mathrm{R}h_{*}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M and pDRh†M≃Rh!pDRM\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}h_{\dagger}M\simeq\mathrm{R}h_{!}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M into account.

Given a 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module MM on a complex manifold (resp. smooth algebraic variety) XX, we denote by HdRk​(X,M)\mathrm{H}^{k}_{\mathrm{dR}}(X,M) the hypercohomology in degree kk of the analytic (resp. algebraic) de Rham complex of MM. Note that here we do not shift the de Rham complex as it is usually done in the theory of 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules. When dealing with an affine variety XX, we will identify algebraic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-modules with their global sections.

Let j:U⸦→Xj\colon U\mathrel{\lhook\joinrel\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}}X be the open embedding of the complement of a divisor DD on XX. Given a holonomic 𝒟U\mathscr{D}_{U}-module MM, the extension j+​Mj_{+}M is the holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module on which any local equation of DD acts in an invertible way. We denote by j†⁣+​Mj_{{\dagger}+}M the intermediate extension, defined as the maximal 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-submodule of j+​Mj_{+}M that has no quotient supported on DD. For a holonomic 𝒟U\mathscr{D}_{U}-module MM with regular singularities at infinity, the inclusion j†⁣+​M→j+​Mj_{{\dagger}+}M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}j_{+}M corresponds to the natural morphism j!∗pDRM→Rj∗pDRMj_{!{*}}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathrm{R}j_{*}\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M via the shifted de Rham functor.

If h:X→Yh\colon X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}Y is smooth, then h+h^{+} sends holonomic 𝒟Y\mathscr{D}_{Y}-modules to holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-modules. This functor corresponds to the usual pullback of vector bundles with connection. If j:U⸦→Xj\colon U\mathrel{\lhook\joinrel\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}}X is an open embedding, then j+j^{+} is the usual restriction functor from holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-modules to holonomic 𝒟U\mathscr{D}_{U}-modules.

Instrumental for the theory of mixed Hodge modules [54] is the notion of nearby cycle and vanishing cycle functors ψf\psi_{f} and ϕf\phi_{f} along a function f:X→𝔸1f\colon X\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} on the category of perverse sheaves and holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules on XX. If MM is a holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module, then ψf​M\psi_{f}M and ϕf​M\phi_{f}M are holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-modules supported on f−1​(0)f^{-1}(0), which are defined in terms of the Kashiwara-Malgrange filtration of MM. Both ψf​M\psi_{f}M and ϕf​M\phi_{f}M are equipped with an automorphism T\mathrm{T} and decompose with respect to its eigenvalues. We denote by ψf,λ​M\psi_{f,\lambda}M and ϕf,λ​M\phi_{f,\lambda}M the generalized eigencomponent corresponding to an eigenvalue λ∈𝐂∗\lambda\in\mathbf{C}^{*}. If λ≠1\lambda\neq 1, there is an isomorphism ψf,λ​M≃ϕf,λ​M\psi_{f,\lambda}M\simeq\phi_{f,\lambda}M compatible with T\mathrm{T}, whereas for λ=1\lambda=1 there is a quiver

with the property that the maps exp(2π𝗂var∘can)\exp(2\pi\mathsf{i}\var\circ\can) and exp(2π𝗂can∘var)\exp(2\pi\mathsf{i}\can\circ\var) coincide with the unipotent automorphism T\mathrm{T} on ψf,1​M\psi_{f,1}M and ϕf,1​M\phi_{f,1}M respectively. The nilpotent endomorphisms var∘can\var\circ\can and can∘var\can\circ\var on ψf,1​M\psi_{f,1}M and ϕf,1​M\phi_{f,1}M are denoted by N{\mathrm{N}}. Up to a suitable shift, the nearby and vanishing cycles of a regular holonomic 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module MM correspond to the nearby and vanishing cycles of the perverse sheaf p​DR⁡M\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M.

Given a meromorphic function φ∈Γ(X,𝒪X(∗P))\varphi\in\Gamma(X,\mathscr{O}_{X}(*P)) on XX with pole divisor PP, we set

Eφ=(𝒪X(∗P),d+dφ),E^{\varphi}=(\mathscr{O}_{X}(*P),{\mathrm{d}}+{\mathrm{d}}\varphi),

and we denote by eφ\mathrm{e}^{\varphi} the generator 1∈𝒪X(∗P)1\in\mathscr{O}_{X}(*P) of EφE^{\varphi}. Consider the product 𝔸t1×𝔸τ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{t}\times\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau} of two affine lines with coordinates tt and τ\tau, and denote by ptp_{t} and pτp_{\tau} the projections to the first and the second factors respectively. The Fourier transform of a 𝒟\mathscr{D}-module (or a bounded complex of 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules) MM on the affine line 𝔸τ1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau} is the complex defined as

FTτ⁡M=pt+​(pτ+​M⊗Et​τ).\FT_{\tau}M=p_{t+}(p_{\tau}^{+}M\otimes E^{t\tau}).

If MM is a holonomic 𝐂[τ]⟨∂τ⟩\mathbf{C}[\tau]\langle\partial_{\tau}\rangle-module, then FTτ⁡M\FT_{\tau}M has cohomology concentrated in degree zero (i.e., is a holonomic 𝐂[t]⟨∂t⟩\mathbf{C}[t]\langle\partial_{t}\rangle-module). This yields a functor FTτ:𝖣holb​(𝒟𝔸τ1)→𝖣holb​(𝒟𝔸t1)\FT_{\tau}\colon\mathsf{D}^{\mathrm{b}}_{\mathrm{hol}}(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{\tau}})\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathsf{D}^{\mathrm{b}}_{\mathrm{hol}}(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{t}}). If MM has regular singularities everywhere, including at infinity, then the only singularity of FTτ⁡M\FT_{\tau}M on 𝔸t1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}_{t} is the origin, which is also regular.

Let s:𝔸1×𝔸1→𝔸1s\colon\mathbb{A}^{\!1}\times\mathbb{A}^{\!1}\mathchoice{\longrightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}{\rightarrow}\mathbb{A}^{\!1} denote the sum map. The additive ∗*-convolution M1⋆∗M2M_{1}\star_{*}M_{2} of M1M_{1} and M2M_{2} is the object s+​(M1⊠M2)s_{+}(M_{1}\boxtimes M_{2}) of 𝖣holb​(𝒟𝔸1)\mathsf{D}^{\mathrm{b}}_{\mathrm{hol}}(\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}). This operation is associative and corresponds to derived tensor product through Fourier transformation:

FT⁡(M1⋆∗M2)≃FT⁡M1​⊗L​FT⁡M2=δ+​(FT⁡M1⊠FT⁡M2),\FT(M_{1}\star_{*}M_{2})\simeq\FT M_{1}\overset{\mathrm{L}}{\otimes}\FT M_{2}=\delta^{+}(\FT M_{1}\boxtimes\FT M_{2}),

For holonomic 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules with regular singularities M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}, the cohomologies in non-zero (i.e., negative) degrees of the complex FT⁡M1⊗LFT⁡M2\FT M_{1}\otimes^{\mathrm{L}}\FT M_{2} are supported at the origin of 𝔸1\mathbb{A}^{\!1}, so the corresponding cohomologies of M1⋆∗M2M_{1}\star_{*}M_{2} are constant 𝒟𝔸1\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-modules. A.2. Notation and results from the theory of mixed Hodge modules

Let XX be a smooth complex projective variety, and let MH=(M,F∙​M,ℱ𝐐,α)M^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}=(M,F_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}M,\mathscr{F}_{\mathbf{Q}},\alpha) be the data of a regular holonomic left 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module MM, an increasing good filtration F∙​MF_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}M on MM, a 𝐐\mathbf{Q}-perverse sheaf ℱ𝐐\mathscr{F}_{\mathbf{Q}} on XX, and an isomorphism α:p​DR⁡M⟶∼ℱ𝐂\alpha\colon\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\sim}}{{\longrightarrow}}\mathscr{F}_{\mathbf{C}}. As it is customary, we shall omit α\alpha from the notation. Let Sp\Sp denote the Spencer complex of a right 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module. We say that MHM^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} is a pure polarizable Hodge module of weight ww if the associated right filtered 𝒟X\mathscr{D}_{X}-module

(ωX⊗𝒪XM,ωX⊗𝒪XF∙−dimXM),(\omega_{X}\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}M,\omega_{X}\otimes_{\mathscr{O}_{X}}F_{{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}-\dim X}M),

together with ℱ𝐐\mathscr{F}_{\mathbf{Q}} and the isomorphism Sp⁡(ωX⊗M)=p​DR⁡M≃ℱ𝐂\Sp(\omega_{X}\otimes M)=\raisebox{6.0pt}{$\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{p}$}{\DR}M\simeq\mathscr{F}_{\mathbf{C}} forms a pure polarizable Hodge module of weight ww in the sense of Saito [53, 5.1.6 & 5.2.10] (see also the introduction of loc. cit.). There is a similar definition for left mixed Hodge modules, with the left-to-right correspondence W∙​M↔ωX⊗W∙​MW_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}M\leftrightarrow\omega_{X}\otimes W_{\scriptscriptstyle\bullet}M between weight filtrations. We refer the reader to [54] for the properties of the category 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(X)\MHM(X) of algebraic mixed Hodge modules, which are always assumed to be graded-polarizable. The derived category 𝖣b​(𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(X))\mathsf{D}^{\mathrm{b}}(\MHM(X)) is endowed with a six-functors formalism, and we denote the functors with a lower left index H{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}} in order to keep the category in mind. For example, the pushforward functor f∗H{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}f_{*} by a morphism ff for left mixed Hodge modules is obtained by composing the similar functor for mixed Hodge modules with the side-changing functor. There is a similar definition for other functors. In particular, additive ∗*-convolution of holonomic 𝒟𝔸1\mathscr{D}_{\mathbb{A}^{\!1}}-modules lifts to 𝖬𝖧𝖬⁡(𝔸1)\MHM(\mathbb{A}^{\!1}), see formula (A.5) below. Be aware that some of these functors may not correspond to the corresponding functors on the underlying 𝒟\mathscr{D}-modules: for example, H⊗{}_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{H}}\otimes does not correspond to ⊗L\otimes^{\mathrm{L}} as used above.
